newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr teeters as support swept away.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr teeters as support swept away.

text.p: The Australian dollar teetered on the brink of a major downtrend Thursday after sellers far and wide clattered the currency down to 5-1/2 month lows.
Dealers said massive amounts of funds were sloshing around world exchanges in search of a safe, higher yielding home and the only destination that fit the bill was the U.S. dollar.

"Exporters are hesitant to buy the AUD, importers are keen to sell the crosses and speculators are happy to follow the momentum," said Steve Shuster, forex head at Citibank Australia. "It'll need the US$ to top for the AUD to find a bottom here."
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local dollar had crumpled to US$0.7710/15 from an early US$0.7758/63 and US$0.7768/53 late here Wednesday.
This was actually its lowest local close since March last year, but it had made an intra-day rough of US$0.7680 on August 2 which dealers saw as the technical floor for the currency.
Support had been forthcoming at 77 cents but many felt a challenge of US$0.7680 could not be far away, with potentially ruinous implications for dollar bulls.
"If the AUD breaks that, it cold get very ugly," said Shuster. "There's some big gaps yawning beneath there."
Chart watchers noted the currency was dangerously close to breaching a major uptrend channel that stretched all the way back to September 1993 when the dollar had troughed at 64 cents.
The violation of such a long standing support line would be very bearish and open the way for a downtrend to 75 cents, or even the January 1996 low of 73 cents.

The lurch lower began offshore Wednesday when European pressure snapped two-week old support at US$0.7738. Local banks followed up the break and talk of options-related sales gave an added edge to the bears. They were joined later by Japanese selling of AUD/yen which completed the rout to US$0.7701.
Exporter bids provided some temporary stability but dealers said many were contemplating pulling their bids in the hope of seeing lower levels in the short term.
The dollar was also finding it hard to sustain gains on the crosses, even though offshore investors were fleeing the low-yielding yen and European currencies in droves.
This was partly because importers were busy taking cover and partly due to Japanese investors lightening long positions built up over a year of buying yen/A$ dual currency samurai issues.
Thus the dollar was held back to 91.93/03 yen from an early 92.43 high even though the yen slumped against the US dollar.

The U.S. currency was the darling of investors everywhere as the diverging economic performance of the U.S. compared with Japan and Germany meant interest differentials would favour the dollar for months to come.

The same glow used to surround the Australian dollar, but two cuts in official rates late last year and speculation of another in the pipeline had dulled its lustre and dragged it down from a six-year high of US$0.8212 in barely two months.
Speculation of a rate cut in February had cooled a little recently but was still considered a 50/50 chance given the improvement seen, and expected, in domestic inflation.

Partial data on manufacturing input prices today, for instance, showed a 0.4 percent fall in November, taking the annual drop to 3.5 percent. Import prices were unchanged for the month and no less than 6.5 percent down on the year.

The key consumer price figures for the December quarter are due next Wednesday and are expected how underlying inflation slowed to 2.2 percent from 2.4 percent in Q3 and a high of 3.3 percent a year ago.
The Reserve Bank policy board meets to decide on February 4 and it was hard to see a let-up in the rate pressure before then. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
